clinicalPearls: A cystic dilatation of the terminal intravesical ureter, classified as intravesical (orthotopic), lying entirely within the bladder, or ectopic, extending into the bladder neck or urethra

In children, ectopic ureteroceles most often arise from the upper-pole moiety of a duplex system, in accordance with the Weigert-Meyer rule (the upper-pole ureter inserts inferomedially and is prone to obstruction/ureterocele, the lower-pole ureter inserts superolaterally and tends to reflux)
In adults, simple orthotopic ureteroceles are usually associated with single systems and may be incidental
May present with antenatal hydronephrosis, urinary tract infection, obstruction, a palpable mass, or, in girls, prolapse of an ectopic ureterocele through the urethra
On urography a ureterocele can produce the classic cobra-head or spring-onion appearance
Large ureteroceles can obstruct the ipsilateral moiety, the contralateral ureter, or the bladder outlet

Management options include endoscopic incision/puncture for decompression, upper-pole heminephrectomy for a non-functioning moiety, and ureteric reimplantation or complete reconstruction depending on function, reflux, and anatomy
reference.pathophysiology: A ureterocele is thought to result from a developmental failure of the terminal ureteric membrane (Chwalla's membrane) to resorb normally, together with abnormal muscular development of the distal ureter, producing a cystic ballooning of the intravesical ureter beneath the bladder mucosa. In duplex systems the upper-pole ureter drains more caudally and medially and is the segment that typically forms an obstructing ureterocele, following the Weigert-Meyer rule. The dilated terminal sac can obstruct urine drainage from its own moiety and, when large or ectopic, may distort the bladder base and outlet, causing wider urinary tract dysfunction and predisposing to infection and upper-tract deterioration.
additionalDifferentials: Bladder diverticulum or cyst near the trigone
Pseudoureterocele from a bladder tumour or oedema around the orifice
Vesicoureteric reflux in a duplex lower moiety
additionalInvestigations: Renal and bladder ultrasound to identify the intravesical cyst and duplex anatomy
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) to assess reflux and ureterocele configuration
MAG3 or DMSA renography to assess function of the affected moiety
Cystoscopy to define the ureterocele and orifice anatomy
MR urography in complex duplex anatomy
Urinalysis and culture when infection is present
redFlags: Bladder outlet obstruction or urinary retention from a large ectopic ureterocele
Prolapse of an ectopic ureterocele through the urethra in a girl
Febrile urinary tract infection or urosepsis with obstruction
Deteriorating function of the affected or contralateral renal unit
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends on the function of the affected moiety and on associated reflux and obstruction; simple orthotopic ureteroceles often do well with endoscopic or conservative management, while complex ectopic duplex ureteroceles may require staged reconstruction but generally preserve overall renal function with appropriate treatment.
pitfalls: Forgetting the Weigert-Meyer rule and misidentifying which moiety the ureterocele drains
Endoscopic incision creating iatrogenic reflux into the decompressed moiety
Overlooking obstruction of the contralateral ureter or bladder outlet by a large ureterocele
Assuming a poorly functioning upper pole must be removed without confirming function
